hints: At M, differentiate the given product with the product and chain rules and set the derivative to zero.
Cancel the non-zero exponential factor and reduce the stationary condition to 2sin²(2x)+4sin(2x)−1=0.
Solve the quadratic in sin2x and use the stated curve domain to select the single x-coordinate, to 3 significant figures.
walkthrough:
Differentiate $y = \mathrm{e}^{\sin(2x)}\cos(4x)$ with respect to $x$ using the product rule:
$$u = \mathrm{e}^{\sin(2x)} \implies \dfrac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x} = 2\cos(2x)\mathrm{e}^{\sin(2x)}$$
$$v = \cos(4x) \implies \dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x} = -4\sin(4x)$$
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 2\cos(2x)\cos(4x)\mathrm{e}^{\sin(2x)} - 4\sin(4x)\mathrm{e}^{\sin(2x)} = \mathrm{e}^{\sin(2x)}\left[2\cos(2x)\cos(4x) - 4\sin(4x)\right]$$

Set the derivative equal to 0 at the stationary point $M$. Since $\mathrm{e}^{\sin(2x)} > 0$ for all real $x$:
$$2\cos(2x)\cos(4x) - 4\sin(4x) = 0$$
$$\cos(2x)\cos(4x) - 2\sin(4x) = 0$$

Substitute $\cos(4x) = 1 - 2\sin^2(2x)$ into the brackets:
$$\cos(2x)\left[1 - 2\sin^2(2x) - 4\sin(2x)\right] = 0$$
$$2\sin^2(2x) + 4\sin(2x) - 1 = 0 \quad (\text{since } \cos(2x) = 0 \implies x = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \text{ is a boundary point})$$

Select the valid root in the interval $0 \leqslant x \leqslant \dfrac{1}{4}\pi \implies 0 \leqslant 2x \leqslant \dfrac{1}{2}\pi \implies 0 \leqslant \sin(2x) \leqslant 1$:
$$\text{Since } -1 - \dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{2} < 0, \text{ take } \sin(2x) = \dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{2} - 1 \approx 1.224745 - 1 = 0.224745$$
